data: Earth–Mars launch windows open every 26 months — driven by orbital resonance. Miss the window and wait two years.

The highest eccentricity of the inner planets (e=0.093) — Mars swings ~20% farther from the Sun at aphelion than at perihelion, driving big seasonal and dust-storm swings. Launch windows, by contrast, are set by the ~26-month Earth–Mars synodic period.
Mariner 4 / 6 / 7 / 9 — NASA, 1965–72 (first flybys then first Mars orbiter, global mapping)
Viking 1 + 2 — NASA, 1976 (first successful Mars landings; biology experiments)
Mars Pathfinder + Sojourner — NASA, 1997 (first wheeled rover on another planet)
Mars Global Surveyor + Odyssey + Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter — NASA, 1997– (multi-decade orbital coverage; MRO HiRise)
Mars Express + ExoMars TGO — ESA, 2003– / 2016– (mineralogy, methane search)
Spirit + Opportunity — NASA, 2004 (twin rovers; Opportunity lasted 14 years)
Phoenix — NASA, 2008 (north polar lander; first to touch water ice)
Curiosity / MSL — NASA, 2012– (Gale crater; nuclear-powered rover, still operating)
Mars Orbiter Mission (Mangalyaan) — ISRO, 2014–22 (India's first interplanetary mission)
Tianwen-1 + Zhurong — CNSA, 2021 (China's first orbital + rover combination)
Perseverance + Ingenuity — NASA, 2021– (Jezero crater; first powered flight on another planet)
ExoMars Rosalind Franklin — ESA, scheduled 2028 launch
Mars's 25.2° axial tilt is remarkably close to Earth's — but combined with its eccentricity, southern summers are intensely hot and short while northern summers are long and mild.
Mars's 0.0935 eccentricity (six times Earth's) gives a 20 % swing in solar flux per orbit — the engine behind global dust storms that can engulf the planet for months.
Mars launch windows open every 26 months — the synodic period between Mars and Earth — and Hohmann transfer is why every Mars mission departs in one of those windows.
Mars has two small captured-looking moons — Phobos (orbiting below synchronous altitude, spiraling inward) and Deimos (slowly receding).
Mars hosts the densest active spacecraft census beyond Earth — orbiters from five agencies and surface rovers / landers from three.
Why Earth has seasons, why Uranus rolled onto its side, and why Venus spins backward.
How stretched the orbit is — zero is a perfect circle, one is a parabolic escape.
The cheapest two-burn trip between two coplanar circular orbits — and the baseline mission planners measure everything else against.
Galileo's four-night observation in 1610 ended geocentrism. The system's moons are still ending old assumptions today.
What's at each planet right now: from MRO at Mars to Juno at Jupiter — while Venus has had no orbiter since Akatsuki ended in 2025.
